title: Rethinking Smartphone Bans: A Smarter Approach to Digital Citizenship in Schools al-citizenship-in-schools-f2334e85ad5e
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek takes up the K-12 debate over banning student smartphones and argues that school leaders should resist an outright ban in favour of building digital citizenship. He accepts that phones can harm the mental health of children under 16, but contends that bans are a bandaid that ends when the school day does. He lists the costs he sees: unequal enforcement, lost learning uses, student resentment and a missed teaching opportunity. His alternative is data-led policy that starts from the actual pain points of students and teachers and is written with their input. The post closes with a practical menu of phone-free zones, a digital wellness curriculum, student-led campaigns and expert partnerships. It is a school-policy argument and a clear case of the pro-balance side of the phone-ban debate.
points: Marcinek's central claim is that a ban treats a symptom, since students simply return to the same habits once the phone is handed back after school.
He argues bans are enforced inequitably, falling hardest on marginalized students, and can worsen school climate and achievement gaps.
He advises leaders to collect data on real pain points, share it, seek student feedback and only then write policy.
His practical alternative combines collaborative policy drafting, designated phone-free zones and an explicit digital wellness curriculum covering privacy, cyberbullying and source verification.
He notes that marginalized students often find community through their phones, so removing access can cost them a real connection.
quotes: Rather than starting with a ban, school leaders should take a hard look at where the pain points are for students and teachers. Once this data is collected, it should be shared, feedback solicited, and policy should follow.

Moreover, these are not wholesale bans for smartphones either, just when they are in school. Once students get their phones back at the end of the day, they have the option to resort back to bad habits.

A ban can look good and feel good with a small sample size, but is it creating new behaviors in the long term? And is it sustainable? In most cases, including the story linked above, the ban approach is only a bandaid to a problem that persists beyond classroom hours.

Phone bans often result in disproportionate enforcement, with students from marginalized backgrounds more likely to be targeted. This can worsen existing achievement gaps and contribute to a negative school climate.
Involve students, parents, teachers, and administrators in drafting a smartphone policy. This will encourage buy-in and create guidelines that work for everyone within your school community.

Rather than resorting to simplistic bans, schools need to invest in equipping students with the necessary skills to navigate our increasingly digital world. By emphasizing digital citizenship, we empower students to become responsible, ethical, and self-aware technology users.

Yes, I am in 100% agreement that smartphones in the hands of children under 16 can cause an array of mental health and social-emotional issues. But if we are not teaching and holding students accountable now, when will they learn appropriate use of technology?
